frictionVectors.title: European energy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies while pressing Algiers to expand exports and manage migration cooperation. Algeria is using market access to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major role in construction, transport, and industrial projects, but the Algerian state continues to tightly regulate strategic assets and foreign participation.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese debt and project exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil-backed financing and Chinese-built infrastructure continue to shape Angola's fiscal room and procurement choices. Luanda is seeking broader Western, Gulf, and Indian partnerships to reduce concentration risk.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore production constraints
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields, declining output, and high operating costs limit the state's ability to convert petroleum reserves into durable sovereign leverage. New investment is essential but can dilute local control.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's trade and customs revenue remain heavily tied to the Port of Cotonou and commercial flows involving Nigeria. External port operators and regional policy shifts can quickly affect sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from Burkina Faso and Niger is increasing pressure on northern Benin, forcing greater reliance on foreign security assistance, intelligence, and border infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong institutional control over diamonds but remains exposed to global price cycles and the commercial influence of major producers and trading networks. The state is pushing for greater domestic sorting and beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other strategic minerals is expanding, bringing investment and infrastructure opportunities alongside pressure to offer favorable terms to foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty drive
frictionVectors.details: The military government is tightening oversight of gold production, refining, and export channels to capture more value and reduce dependence on foreign mining companies. This risks investor flight, sanctions exposure, and operational disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer security ties with Russia and the broader Alliance of Sahel States reduce Western influence but increase dependence on opaque external security networks. Persistent insurgency continues to restrict access to mining zones and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining governance and external capital
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking investment in nickel, gold, and rare-earth prospects while retaining weak oversight capacity. Contract opacity and limited local processing leave the state vulnerable to value leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border and logistics pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed-group accusations and border restrictions. Dependence on neighboring corridors increases Burundi's exposure to political disruption and higher transport costs.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and renewable-energy projects rely heavily on foreign finance and operators. This improves connectivity but limits domestic leverage over critical assets and long-term revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location makes it important for counter-narcotics, fisheries enforcement, and transatlantic logistics. External security partnerships are valuable but create dependence on foreign surveillance and naval capacity.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and mining remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector dependence and opaque concessions
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, and emerging mining projects attract Chinese, European, and other foreign operators. Weak transparency and limited domestic refining or processing reduce Cameroon’s ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and transport disruption
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, plantations, energy assets, and public administration. Instability also raises the cost of the Kribi-Douala logistics corridor and deters domestic investment.

highlights: Gold and diamonds remain weakly governed

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security-for-resource leverage
frictionVectors.details: The government remains heavily dependent on Russian-linked security support, which strengthens regime survival but narrows policy autonomy. Mining access and political influence are closely intertwined with the security relationship.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict corridors and illicit mining
frictionVectors.details: Gold, diamonds, and timber move through poorly controlled borderlands toward neighboring markets. Armed groups, foreign networks, and weak state infrastructure limit formal revenue collection and territorial control.

highlights: Oil revenues anchor a security state
Sahel and Sudan spillovers intensify pressure

frictionVectors.title: Oil infrastructure and external bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chad depends on foreign technical, financial, and export infrastructure for its oil sector, leaving production and revenue vulnerable to external commercial decisions. Limited diversification weakens sovereign leverage over fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Border insecurity and foreign military influence
frictionVectors.details: War in Sudan and instability across Libya and the Central African Republic place sustained pressure on Chad’s borders and humanitarian systems. N'Djamena continues balancing relationships with France, Russia-linked actors, Gulf states, and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains effective control of Mayotte, sustaining a major sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros's influence over surrounding maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: External aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Budget support, remittances, and infrastructure financing from France, Gulf states, and other partners constrain policy autonomy while domestic resource capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-linked conflict and mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: M23 activity and regional military competition continue to threaten territorial control in the east, where illicit mineral flows and cross-border logistics weaken Kinshasa's sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and Gulf actors are competing for strategic minerals and infrastructure access, while weak contract enforcement limits the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export earnings remain highly exposed to oil production and price volatility, reducing leverage over foreign operators and limiting diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and extractive projects expand connectivity but create repayment and strategic-dependence concerns around national infrastructure.

highlights: Abidjan emerges as a regional hub

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-sector external capture
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening local processing and producer oversight, but multinational buyers and volatile global prices still capture much of the cocoa value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and transport expansion attracts French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors, creating opportunities while requiring careful management of long-term concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Great-power military footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and security but make Djibouti's strategic space heavily dependent on external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked port and rail infrastructure strengthens the country's logistics role while sustaining concerns over debt, concession control, and dependence on external trade flows.

highlights: Suez Canal remains a strategic revenue chokepoint

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Water Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating agreement for the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and Gulf investment support fiscal stability but increase outside leverage over strategic assets, currency policy, and infrastructure priorities.

highlights: China remains a major infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Assets
frictionVectors.details: Falling production and limited diversification are weakening state revenues while foreign operators retain importance in offshore extraction and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain central to transport and public-works projects, creating dependency despite government efforts to preserve full political control.

highlights: Red Sea geography amplifies strategic leverage
State retains tight control over ports and security

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and foreign naval activity increase pressure on Eritrea's coastline, ports, and territorial neutrality.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia Access Demands
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopian interest in reliable Red Sea access remains a persistent sovereignty concern, particularly around Assab and the wider security relationship.

highlights: Economic lifelines run through South Africa
Sugar and logistics remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Most trade, transport, energy, and financial channels are tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room for independent infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Trade Preference Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, textiles, and manufactured exports depend heavily on external market access and preference regimes that can be revised by larger partners.

highlights: Port access remains a strategic vulnerability

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Access Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for dependable maritime access continues to generate tension with coastal neighbors and exposes the country to external bargaining over ports and corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on foreign lenders constrain sovereign control over major infrastructure, even as domestic power generation capacity expands.

highlights: Post-coup authorities consolidate control over oil and manganese
National-content agenda rises amid external investor scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional government is seeking greater state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and timber. Renegotiation risks friction with established French, Chinese, and regional commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port infrastructure remain reliant on foreign capital and operators, limiting Libreville's room to impose rapid changes without disrupting commodity revenues.

highlights: Democratic stability holds, but fiscal sovereignty remains constrained
Fisheries and port access dominate resource-security concerns

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Limited enforcement capacity leaves coastal fisheries vulnerable to illegal, unreported, and unregulated activity. Dependence on external monitoring and maritime assistance complicates full control of national waters.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Roads, energy, and public-finance programs remain heavily supported by international donors and lenders. This provides stability but narrows policy autonomy during fiscal stress.

highlights: Debt restructuring strengthens discipline but limits policy freedom
Gold and emerging lithium sectors face sovereignty tests

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal mining and foreign supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining damages land and water while feeding opaque domestic and foreign trading networks. Enforcement efforts remain politically sensitive because mining supports large numbers of livelihoods.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Potential lithium development is drawing international interest before Ghana has fully established processing, taxation, and local-content safeguards. The risk is renewed export dependence with limited domestic value capture.

highlights: Junta-led mining expansion prioritizes bauxite and Simandou

frictionVectors.title: Simandou and rail corridor control
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is reshaping Guinea's strategic infrastructure and export outlook, but financing, rail access, and consortium arrangements give foreign partners substantial leverage over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite dependence and local discontent
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite revenues remain central while environmental damage, land pressure, and limited domestic processing fuel grievances. The military government faces pressure to convert mining scale into broader national benefits.

highlights: Political fragility leaves ports and fisheries exposed
External security and narcotics networks shape state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and maritime access
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement make fisheries, port operations, and coastal resources vulnerable to foreign exploitation. Dependence on outside technical and security support constrains sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Transnational narcotics influence
frictionVectors.details: The country's position between Latin America and Europe continues to attract trafficking networks that can penetrate political and security institutions. This undermines fiscal capacity and makes infrastructure and customs governance especially vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial external debt limit Nairobi's room to set independent spending and industrial policy. Chinese lending remains strategically important, even as Kenya seeks broader financing partners.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The Mombasa and Lamu corridors attract Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interest because of their regional access. Security costs, local land grievances, and competition with neighboring ports complicate Kenya's effort to retain full strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: HIGHLANDS WATER PROJECT
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains Lesotho's dominant buyer and infrastructure partner for bulk water, creating dependable revenue but significant bargaining asymmetry. Construction, royalties, and environmental impacts remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: ECONOMIC CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's labor market, trade routes, and manufacturing base are deeply tied to South Africa. This dependence limits sovereign leverage when Pretoria adjusts border, customs, or labor policies.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital and concession operators, leaving Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and uneven revenue capture. Contract transparency and local-content demands remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: EXPORT CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and investors retain major influence over port, rail, and mining logistics. Liberia's ability to negotiate better terms is constrained by limited domestic infrastructure and fiscal dependence.

frictionVectors.title: OIL INSTITUTIONAL SPLIT
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security centers continue to contest control over oil revenues, production decisions, and state institutions. Disruptions or threats to fields, terminals, and the central bank can rapidly become national power struggles.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY SPONSORS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked networks, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and European actors retain influence through military, political, or energy relationships. Their competing interests reduce Libya's ability to secure unified control of its infrastructure and borders.

frictionVectors.title: MINING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining operations provide exports and employment but leave Madagascar dependent on external technology, capital, and commodity demand. Tax terms, environmental damage, and local benefit-sharing remain contentious.

frictionVectors.title: LAND AND INFRASTRUCTURE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, ports, and agricultural land attract competing foreign commercial interests while local communities contest displacement and weak consultation. Limited state capacity makes enforcement of environmental and labor standards uneven.

highlights: Mining and energy security move up the agenda

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concessions and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects offer badly needed revenue but may limit domestic value capture. IMF-linked fiscal reforms further narrow the government's room to negotiate.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Fuel Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and imported fuel expose Malawi to external price shocks and constrain industrial development.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel reduces Western leverage but risks opaque arrangements involving strategic assets and mining interests.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector and Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and industrial gold production is undermined by insurgent taxation, smuggling, and weak state oversight, limiting sovereign revenue capture.

highlights: Iron and hydrogen projects attract major capital

frictionVectors.title: Gas Revenue and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas development can strengthen fiscal autonomy, but foreign operators and cross-border arrangements will determine how much value remains in Mauritania.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Land and Power
frictionVectors.details: Large externally financed hydrogen schemes raise questions over land access, transmission infrastructure, water use, and domestic industrial benefits.

highlights: Import dependence remains the core vulnerability

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Maritime Jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos issue remains central to Mauritius's territorial sovereignty and maritime-resource claims, requiring careful management of external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Food Imports
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, food, and industrial inputs leaves the island exposed to shipping disruptions and foreign price volatility.

highlights: Industrial policy captures more mineral value
Renewables and ports reinforce regional leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure activity in Western Sahara continues to generate legal and diplomatic friction over consent, sovereignty, and external commercial involvement.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and other investors support ports, renewables, and industry, while raising concerns about dependence and control of critical networks.

highlights: LNG restart remains central to fiscal recovery
Cabo Delgado security still limits resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and private-security dependence continue to constrain Maputo's control over northern gas assets. Foreign operators retain substantial leverage over project timing and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: External investors are expanding positions in graphite and other minerals, while weak local processing capacity limits domestic value capture.

highlights: Oil and green-hydrogen ambitions are accelerating

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Major discoveries have increased competition among international energy firms for offshore blocks. Namibia is seeking greater state participation and local benefits without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Green-Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed projects require major transmission, port, and water investments. Financing and export dependence could limit sovereign control over the emerging sector.

highlights: Sovereignty-first policy is reshaping foreign partnerships
Security and export bottlenecks threaten resource revenues

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are renegotiating or reassessing longstanding foreign mining relationships, especially in uranium. Institutional uncertainty and sanctions risk could reduce investment and production.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor
frictionVectors.details: The cross-border pipeline to the Benin coast is strategically vital but vulnerable to diplomatic rupture and regional insecurity. Limited alternative infrastructure leaves Niger exposed to external transit leverage.

highlights: Energy reforms aim to restore state and investor confidence
Domestic processing is expanding but unevenly

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Sector Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, pipeline insecurity, and opaque contracting continue to weaken public capture of petroleum wealth. International operators retain significant technical and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Refining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: New refining capacity could reduce import dependence, but gas infrastructure and financing remain closely tied to foreign capital and equipment supply chains.

highlights: State capacity remains strong and coordinated

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda benefits from mineral flows linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo create sustained diplomatic and sanctions exposure. International scrutiny threatens Kigali's access to premium markets and external finance.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Technology Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong domestic control over infrastructure and development planning, but remains sensitive to donor conditions and foreign technology dependence.

frictionVectors.title: UNCERTAIN HYDROCARBON SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in São Tomé and Príncipe's maritime zones has attracted external interest, but commercial production remains unconfirmed. Limited state capacity increases dependence on foreign technical and legal expertise.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies on regional and external partners to monitor its large maritime domain against illegal fishing and trafficking. This creates recurring sovereignty concerns over surveillance access and security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN OPERATOR LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas production offers fiscal upside but remains dependent on international operators, export infrastructure, and foreign financing. Contract reviews and demands for greater local participation risk investor friction.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND ENERGY FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and power projects remain exposed to debt pressures and external lenders, including Gulf, Chinese, European, and multilateral actors. The government is balancing strategic autonomy against the need for rapid capital deployment.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SURVEILLANCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on partners such as India, France, and other international actors for maritime-domain awareness and anti-piracy support. Assistance improves control over its exclusive economic zone but also embeds external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external tourism cycles, imported energy costs, and climate-related disruption. Dependence on foreign capital for resorts, ports, and renewable infrastructure can narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects remain central to foreign-exchange earnings, with overseas firms controlling capital, technology, and export logistics. The government faces pressure to improve fiscal returns while avoiding disruptions to investment.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: External financing and operators are shaping port, road, and logistics infrastructure linked to mineral exports. These arrangements can improve connectivity but may lock the country into commodity-centered development and long-term concession obligations.

highlights: Ports and offshore resources draw rivals

frictionVectors.title: PORT CONCESSION COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Gulf actors, and other partners compete for influence over ports, logistics, and security relationships. Divergent federal and member-state deals complicate unified control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE RESOURCE AND SECURITY RISK
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore oil and gas development is constrained by insecurity, contested maritime authority, and limited regulatory capacity. Al-Shabaab attacks and fragmented governance raise the cost of protecting infrastructure and negotiating credible contracts.

frictionVectors.title: MINING OWNERSHIP AND PROCESSING
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and leverage over platinum, manganese and other strategic minerals, while foreign capital remains essential for investment and technology.

frictionVectors.title: ELECTRICITY AND LOGISTICS
frictionVectors.details: Grid reliability, rail bottlenecks and congested ports weaken sovereign control over export corridors and increase dependence on private operators and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: OIL EXPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Nearly all state revenue depends on oil moving through Sudanese infrastructure, leaving Juba exposed to pipeline disruption, transit bargaining and foreign operator influence.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Armed rivalries and cross-border networks constrain government control over production zones, roads and border trade while neighboring states retain significant leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SMUGGLING AND EXTERNAL SPONSORSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and commercial networks contest gold-producing areas, with external buyers and financiers weakening any unified national resource regime.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan and oil-export infrastructure, enabling neighboring states and foreign actors to gain leverage over humanitarian access, trade and energy flows.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for greater state participation, local processing and revenue capture in gold, graphite and nickel projects, creating friction with multinational investors.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Expansion around Dar es Salaam and regional rail links increases Tanzania's strategic value, but external lenders, contractors and neighboring commercial interests remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a Gulf of Guinea transshipment and landlocked-market hub strengthens national leverage, but port expansion and logistics remain reliant on foreign capital and operators.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: The state retains strategic influence over phosphate resources, while production performance, financing needs and external buyers constrain its ability to convert reserves into broader sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Finance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress limits Tunis's bargaining power and increases dependence on external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Declining phosphate performance and reliance on imported hydrocarbons weaken domestic resource sovereignty. Energy partnerships may stabilize supply but can narrow Tunisian control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil corridor remains central to export ambitions but faces external financing, environmental, and sanctions-related pressure. Foreign operators and lenders retain substantial influence over project timing and terms.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand Uganda's infrastructure base while increasing repayment and procurement dependence. Debt obligations could constrain future control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: International mining firms remain dominant in extraction, processing, and financing despite stronger government efforts to raise state participation. Copper price volatility and investor pressure can limit Lusaka's ability to impose local-value requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is balancing Chinese mining and infrastructure ties with expanding Western and Gulf interest in critical minerals. This competition creates leverage for Lusaka but also risks fragmented standards and concession politics.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is seeking domestic processing and tighter controls on lithium and other minerals, but foreign capital and technology remain essential. Chinese firms retain a particularly strong position across mining and refining projects.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Currency Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions exposure and chronic currency instability restrict access to finance and push the government toward opaque bilateral arrangements. These conditions weaken oversight and reduce the state's ability to capture full resource value.
